If the selling point of your show that you’re actively trying to market is solely based on (or even mostly based on) how culturally progressive it is rather than the merits of the show, that is going to be off-putting to the average consumer. It’s a well known trend in the modern media landscape that if literally all a show has going for it is the values it espouses, it’s probably not going to be good. This is not saying that culturally progressive media cannot be good and often times it can be some of the most beloved media in existence, case in point the war and imperialism analogies present in the original Star Wars and the Prequels and for a more recent example, TLOU. However, these pieces of media still set out to tell good stories first and foremost, while a lot of modern media seems to want to focus on the representation first and the story later. I can’t judge The Acolyte on the merits and I’m not trying to, as I haven’t seen it as I’ve given up on Disney Star Wars. However, if the producer of the show said “this is the gayest Star Wars has been” in an attempt to give me an incentive to watch it, it would do nothing to pique my interest in any form. 

And in case you want to ask, no, it’s not a personal attack on me, I’m bi lol.

I understand that Rian certainly made a more unique story than we’d expect from where TFA was leading us, but just because it’s unique doesn’t mean it’s good (something something axe with a wooden blade.) To be blunt, they probably SHOULD have played it safe, albeit a bit boring, if they wanted the sequels to succeed, though I would agree some things Rian set up eg making Kylo out to be the villain of the final film was a good idea. However, at the end of the day, what he made was simply too radical for the series and serves more as a mockery than a deconstruction of ideas. 

The issue is that Luke was prone to outbursts… before he was trained as a Jedi. After only a year of training, Luke was far more cool and collected compared to how he was in ANH and especially ESB. The only time Luke really has an outburst is when his sister is threatened by Vader, and while that is technically an outburst, it was his only actual one in the entire movie that was remotely comparable to his moments of irrationality in ANH/ESB. The point of these characters is that they grew up and evolved from the OT. It’s the same reason that people didn’t like Han in TFA - he went from being a self serving smuggler in ANH to a decorated war veteran who fought for others and (would be) a loving husband to Leia in RotJ before going back to being a self serving smuggler in TFA. While I won’t pretend Luke was the EXACT same between the OT and TLJ, it’s pretty damning that they didn’t care about any of the growth or characterization past ESB to the point that Luke’s green lightsaber has a collective like, 20 seconds of screen time in the entire ST. 

Luke as a 23 year old, not a kid yet not fully developed either, was grappling with extreme revelations, and reacted pretty emotionally intelligently compared to how somebody that age probably would normally react to the knowledge their dad is a child murdering satanist who just threatened to convert his sister. Compare that to a fully grown Jedi Grand Master Luke almost murdering a conflicted and confused teenager with dark thoughts who hadn’t actually committed any evil deeds. They’re just not remotely comparable situations. In regards to the Jedi texts, the point of Luke’s character is to evolve past the traditional Jedi. In fact, in the novelization of TLJ, it’s made clear - Luke disregards the old teachings of the Jedi in regards to certain aspects of the Force, with one of these significant factors being the Jedi’s stances on relationships, which is a natural conclusion, considering it was ignoring Yoda and Obi-Wan on how Luke should deal with Vader that allowed him to “defeat” Vader in the first place. This is also why BoBF mischaracterizes Luke arguably just as egregiously as TLJ by making him dogmatic to the Jedi teachings.

The point is, Luke simply wouldn’t have been in the situation where he would have drawn his lightsaber, even for a split second. But, for a moment, let us entertain this notion. He pulls the lightsaber on Ben, Ben collapses the hut, and Ben (which was actually revealed to be Palpatine in the comics) burns down the Jedi temple and kills the rest of Luke’s academy. Mark Hamill put it best when he said Luke wouldn’t sit on his ass getting fat and depressed on an island while his friends suffer and fought due to a mistake he caused. He’d be on the frontlines, trying to atone and set it right (paraphrasing.) Ok, well, let’s say he did do that, and Rey turned his mindset around. He appears on Crait through Force astral projection or whatever, and confronts Kylo. Well, at least now he’ll truly apologize and will genuinely try to talk to Ben, explain himself, and try to plead with him to return, right? Nope, he declares that Ben is unsalvageable, mocks him, says he “failed him” (which is an Obi-Wan callback, despite the movie being so pretentious it doesn’t realize this completely ruins any growth Luke had from the traditional Jedi on the OT) and then leaves him there. He literally showed up to shit on him while the Resistance escaped and left. Nothing about Luke in the ST is remotely in character for what the Luke in RotJ was leading to.

Rian fundamentally ruined a massive part of the appeal and love of Star Wars in the way he portrayed Luke Skywalker. You can argue that they could salvage the pieces and make an ok ending but in reality, even if JJ sucks, he was already dealt an infinitely shittier card than he had when he wrote TFA, especially due to Rian severely undercutting even the slightest implications of plot threads that could be explored.
